name: Zechariah
bio:
Zechariah, grandson of Iddo (called here simply "son of Iddo"), together with Haggai the prophet, prophesied to the Jews of Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, encouraging Zerubbabel and Jeshua to resume building the temple after years of delay; the two prophets helped them as the work went forward (Ezra 5:1-2). His own visions and messages are recorded in full in the book that bears his name. Through their prophesying, the elders of the Jews prospered in the work and finished the temple in the sixth year of Darius, dedicating it with joy (Ezra 6:14-16).

## 📖 Core Story: Visions of Restoration

In the second year of Darius, Zechariah son of Berechiah received a series of eight night visions: horsemen patrolling the earth, four horns representing nations that had scattered Judah broken by four craftsmen, a man measuring Jerusalem for rebuilding, the high priest Joshua's filthy garments replaced with clean ones while Satan's accusations were rebuked (a sign pointing to the coming "Branch"), a golden lampstand flanked by Zerubbabel and Joshua as "the two anointed ones," a flying scroll of judgment, a woman representing wickedness carried off to Babylon, and four chariots patrolling the earth's four directions (Zechariah 1:1-6:8). He then had crowns made and placed on Joshua's head as a sign of the priest-king figure to come, who would build the LORD's temple (Zechariah 6:9-15). When envoys asked whether ritual fasting for Jerusalem's destruction should continue, Zechariah relayed God's answer that true fasting means true justice and mercy, not empty ritual, and promised that Jerusalem would again be filled with celebration and old people and children playing safely in its streets, with Jews gathered back from every nation (Zechariah 7:1-8:23).

## 📖 Core Story: The Coming King and the Good Shepherd Rejected

In oracles concerning the nations and Jerusalem's future, Zechariah foretold a king who would come to Zion humble, riding on a donkey, bringing peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:9-10) — a prophecy later understood to point to the Messiah. He described a good shepherd rejected by his own flock and paid off with thirty pieces of silver, thrown into the temple and given to a potter — language the Gospels later tied to Judas's betrayal of Jesus (Zechariah 11:4-17). He also foresaw a day when Jerusalem's inhabitants would look on one "whom they have pierced" and mourn deeply, as one mourns an only child, followed by a cleansing fountain opened for sin (Zechariah 12:1-13:9). The book closes with a vision of the LORD himself coming to fight for Jerusalem, splitting the Mount of Olives, becoming king over all the earth, and making even Jerusalem's cooking pots as holy as the temple's sacred vessels (Zechariah 14:1-21).
